title: Foundation Cracks and Water Seepage: Structural or Moisture? | Gold Water Fire, Phoenix, AZ
description: How to read foundation cracks and slab seepage in Arizona homes, and how to tell a structural movement problem from a moisture problem before you spend money.
h1: Foundation Cracks, Water Seepage & Telling a Structural Problem From a Moisture One
intro: You have probably been looking at the same spot for a while now. A hairline running out from the corner of a doorway. A patch of baseboard that stays dark after everything else has dried. Carpet in one corner of a room that feels cooler underfoot than it should. You mopped it, you caulked it, you told yourself it was the last big rain, and then it came back. What makes this kind of thing hard is not the damage itself, it is not knowing what it means. A crack could be nothing. It could also be the visible edge of something moving underneath your house. Until you know which one you are dealing with, every repair feels like a guess, and the not-knowing sits with you longer than the water does.

sections.heading: Two different problems that look almost identical
sections.body:
A structural problem is a movement problem. The soil under a slab expands, shrinks, or settles unevenly, and the concrete above it has to go somewhere. It cracks, tilts, or separates. Water is often present, but it is a passenger, not the driver.

A moisture problem is a water-path problem. The slab is doing fine. Water is simply finding a way to the inside: through a cold joint, a control joint, a penetration where plumbing comes up through the concrete, a failed exterior grade that sends runoff toward the house instead of away, or a slow supply line leak under the slab.

The reason people go in circles for months is that both show up in the same places, along baseboards, at slab edges, in the corners of rooms, and both produce a crack you can put a fingernail into. Telling them apart is less about the crack and more about the pattern around it: what else moved, what else got wet, and when.

cards.heading: Signs pointing toward movement
cards.body: Doors and windows that stick or swing on their own, cracks that step diagonally up from the corners of door and window openings, gaps opening between wall and ceiling or wall and floor, cracked tile that runs in a line across multiple tiles rather than one, a floor that is visibly out of level, and cracks that are wider at one end than the other.

cards.heading: Signs pointing toward moisture only
cards.body: Damp lines that rise a few inches up drywall and stop, white chalky mineral deposits on concrete, flooring adhesive letting go, musty smell strongest at floor level, staining that changes with rain or irrigation, and cracks that stay the same width while the wetness comes and goes.

cards.heading: Signs that are honestly both
cards.body: A hairline crack in a slab with a little dampness in it tells you almost nothing on its own. Concrete cracks as it cures. So does stucco. The question is whether it is changing. A static crack that never widens and never weeps is different from one you can watch season by season.

sections.heading: Why this happens the way it does in the Phoenix valley
sections.body:
Desert soil does not behave the way people expect. Large parts of the Phoenix metro sit on clay-bearing and collapsible soils. Clay swells when it takes on water and shrinks when it dries, so a slab can be lifted in one season and dropped in the next. Collapsible soils do the opposite: they hold up fine while dry and lose volume suddenly when saturated, which is why a home can go years with nothing and then move after one unusual wet stretch.

The water source is usually closer than people think. Irrigation and drip lines running along a foundation, a lawn watered on a schedule set for July, downspouts dumping at the wall, a rear yard graded flat or sloped back toward the house, and monsoon runoff that arrives faster than the ground can take it. Any of these will keep the soil at one edge of the house wet while the rest of the perimeter stays bone dry, and that difference in moisture is exactly what makes a slab move unevenly.

There is also the plumbing under the concrete. A slab leak in a hot or cold supply line can put water into the soil continuously for months with no puddle anywhere inside. Common tells are a hot spot on the floor, a water heater or system that runs more than it used to, an unexplained jump in the water bill, and the sound of running water when every fixture is off.

sections.heading: What you can do yourself, in order
sections.body:
None of this requires tools you do not already have, and all of it makes any later conversation with a professional shorter and more accurate.

1. Date and mark the crack. Draw a light pencil line across it at two points and write the date. Photograph it with a coin or tape measure in frame. Repeat monthly. A crack that has not changed in six months is a very different animal from one that has.

2. Do the meter test on the water. Turn off every fixture and appliance that uses water, then read the meter, wait two hours with nothing running, and read it again. Movement means water is leaving the system somewhere, and under-slab is a real possibility.

3. Walk the outside after a rain, or after the irrigation runs. Look for standing water within a few feet of the wall, soil that has pulled away from the foundation leaving a gap, downspouts discharging at the base, and any area where grade slopes toward the house rather than away.

4. Tape a square of clear plastic sheeting tightly to the bare slab or concrete floor and leave it a day or two. Moisture on the underside of the plastic points to water coming up through the concrete. Moisture on the room side points to humidity condensing on a cold slab. Those are two different fixes.

5. Check for level. A ball or marble placed on the floor in several rooms will tell you quickly whether one area is out. So will a long straightedge across a doorway threshold.

6. Note the timing. Does the wetness track with rain, with irrigation days, with laundry and showers, or with nothing at all? Water that appears regardless of weather is usually plumbing. Water that appears only after storms is usually grade and drainage.

sections.heading: Why fixing the wrong one first wastes the money
sections.body: If the real issue is soil movement and you patch and paint, the patch will crack again on the same line, because nothing about the cause changed. If the real issue is water intrusion and you go straight to structural repair, you spend a great deal for a house that is still taking on water. The order that generally holds up is: stop the water first, dry the assembly completely, and only then evaluate whether anything actually moved. Drying takes real equipment and real time, because water in concrete, framing, and insulation does not leave on a fan and an open window. Wet materials also read as damage that is not there yet, so an assessment made while everything is still saturated tends to be wrong in both directions. One thing worth being blunt about: wet organic material inside a wall cavity does not stay neutral. Drywall, paper facing, baseboard, and cabinet toe kicks will start to grow given days rather than weeks in a warm house. If a wall has been damp for a while, what is behind it matters more than what is on it. If you get to the point where materials have to come out and go back in, that is water damage restoration followed by reconstruction and rebuild, and it is worth having the same people see both halves so nothing gets closed up wet. If you want a second set of eyes on what you are looking at, you can reach out or read more about who we are.

faqs.q: Is every crack in a slab or foundation a serious problem?
faqs.a: No. Concrete shrinks as it cures and hairline cracking is common in slabs, stucco, and driveways. What matters is whether a crack is changing width, whether it steps diagonally from the corners of doors and windows, whether it is offset so one side sits higher than the other, and whether water comes through it. A crack that is stable and dry over months is very different from one that opens a little more each season.

faqs.q: How can I tell if I have a slab leak versus rain getting in?
faqs.a: Timing is the clearest signal. Rain and irrigation intrusion shows up after water hits the ground outside and fades as things dry. A slab leak keeps producing moisture regardless of weather. Shut off everything that uses water and watch the meter for a couple of hours. If it moves, water is escaping somewhere in the system. A warm patch on the floor or the faint sound of running water with all fixtures off points the same direction.

faqs.q: Do I need a structural engineer or a restoration contractor first?
faqs.a: If the issue is water and the framing, drywall, flooring, and cabinetry are wet, a restoration contractor addresses the water and the drying. If floors are visibly out of level, doors have shifted in their frames, or cracks are offset and widening, a structural engineer is the right person to evaluate the movement. Many homeowners end up needing both, and in that case stopping and drying the water first gives the engineer an accurate picture.

faqs.q: Can moisture coming up through a slab be fixed without tearing out the floor?
faqs.a: It depends on the source. If the water is coming from exterior grade, roof runoff, or irrigation against the foundation, correcting drainage outside can resolve it without touching the interior. If water has already saturated flooring, adhesive, baseboard, and the bottom of the drywall, those materials usually have to be removed to dry the structure properly, because covering wet material traps the moisture instead of solving it.
